After an event, the class of a placement is defined relative to the participant’s own placement on the event trial (t0). A placement is

if enough nets lie within ±2 slots of both the t0 placement and the direction of the displaced attack. In the strategy analyses “enough” is a share of at least .25 of the nets, which with 7 nets means at least 2 nets on each direction.

of questionnaires are per SD of the questionnaire; log-odds for event indicators (logistic GEE clustered by participant), SD of the measure for participant-level measures.

The split class was recomputed with at least 1, 2 (the definition used so far) or 3 of the 7 nets on each direction; the other classes were assigned as before. The table gives the share of events classified as split.
Questionnaire slopes for split placements at t+2 after transitions (log-odds per SD; * p < .05, ** p < .01):

With a single net on each direction, about twice as many placements count as split, and the associations across conditions become weaker (only STICSA state stays below .05). The slopes with Full instructions remain.
With 2 or 3 nets the estimates are similar; with 3 nets the events become rare and the intervals wider.

The associations therefore concern placements with a substantial share of nets on both directions; a single stray net on the second direction does not carry them. All estimates per indicator, threshold and condition:
2  What the entropy associations consist of

children.label: 2  What the entropy associations consist of

children.value: The net entropy of a placement (bits) splits exactly into two parts:
: the entropy of how the nets are divided between separate clusters (0 if all nets form one cluster);
: the entropy of the nets within each cluster, weighted by the cluster’s share of the nets (how wide the clusters are).

In stable and event placements alike, about two thirds of all placements form one cluster. Placements after events form two or more clusters in 36–45 % of the events in None and Partial and in 18–31 % in Full.

The B2 model (outcome ~ condition × event × placement × questionnaire, random intercepts per participant and event) was fitted to each part and to the probability of two or more clusters. The net-entropy slopes reproduce B2 (e.g. STICSA state, oddball t+1: .091, p = .03). Questionnaire slopes (bits per SD; split: log-odds per SD):
0.6 to 1.5 (None oddball t+1; Full t+1 after both events: p < .05)
the entropy associations come from wider clusters. Higher STICSA state, STICSA trait and BDI scores go with nets spread over more consecutive slots, not with nets divided between locations.

higher STICSA state and OCI scores go with more placements that are divided into separate clusters, but those clusters are narrower. The two parts have opposite signs and largely cancel in the net entropy, which is why B2 shows no entropy association in these conditions.

STICSA trait goes with wider clusters: within-cluster entropy .087 bits per SD at oddball t+1 (p = .030), .085 at oddball t+2 (p = .035) and .110 at transition t+2 (p = .009), not at transition t+1 (.035, p = .41). After BH correction across the five questionnaires only transition t+2 remains (q = .047; oddball t+1 and t+2 q = .15 and .17). For STICSA state both parts contribute, and neither alone reaches p < .05.

goes with fewer split placements at t+2 after oddballs (ρ = −.52, p = .013, n = 22), and in Partial a higher α goes with more split placements at t+1 after transitions (ρ = .38, p = .028). File:
4  Error at t+2 after a split placement at t+1

children.label: 4  Error at t+2 after a split placement at t+1

children.value: For each event, the error of the placement at t+2 relative to the target (log(|error| + 1), as in B1) was compared between events with a split placement at t+1 and the participant’s other events (linear mixed model with the split indicator centred within participant, the participant’s split rate, and a random intercept per participant).
Within participants: difference after a split [SE]

After transitions, the error at t+2 tends to be lower when the participant had split the nets at t+1, clearly so without instructions. In degrees (mean of participant means), the error at t+2 after transitions in None was 32° after a split at t+1, 62° after following the displaced attack and 67° after staying at the t0 placement. After oddballs there is no difference. Between participants, the split rate is not related to the t+2 error. Files:
Within an episode, the direction of the second colour cue is that of the first plus 70°. Two measures per participant:

The circular mean placement for cue B minus that for cue A on regular trials from the fourth trial of the episode, as a fraction of 70° (1 = the full offset, 0 = the same direction for both cues). This is the definition of the learned cue offset of the preprocessing, kept per episode. The
from the first episode from which the offset lies between .5 and 1.5 in that episode and in at least 75 % of the remaining episodes. Participant summaries are circular means over episodes.
On the first trial of the other cue after a transition, the deviation of the placement from that cue’s new direction (|I_e|, as in model D; 0 = the transition was carried over to the other cue).
The offset agrees with the learned cue offset (ρ = .97) and with the model parameter cue sensitivity (ρ = .76; median cue sensitivity None .64, Partial .83, Full .94).

Participants without full instructions fall into two groups (

b): about half place the nets for the two cues about 70° apart, the others at about the same direction. In None the offset grows over the session; in Partial it is present from the first episodes on in those who learn it. With full instructions nearly all participants apply the offset from the first episode. Condition contrasts: Full vs None + Partial p < .001 for the offset and for learning; Partial vs None p = .17 and .47.
Transfer after transitions improved over the session only in Full (−3.4° per episode, p = .09) and was weakly related to the offset (ρ = .27).

Higher STICSA trait scores went with a larger offset (β = .21 SD per SD, p = .023, across conditions) and higher STICSA state scores with a smaller increase over the episodes (β = −.19, p = .035). Whether and when the mapping was learned was not associated with any questionnaire, in None + Partial or in all participants (discrete-time hazard of learning, learning episode of those who learn, and learning at all; all p ≥ .21;

). Higher STICSA trait (β = .20, p = .014) and OCI (β = .26, p = .015) scores went with a larger deviation on the first other-cue trial after a transition, i.e. less transfer; within Partial also BDI (β = .28, p = .018) and OCI (β = .23, p = .033). Files:

9  When do the latent states start to fit? Relative fit per episode

children.label: 9  When do the latent states start to fit? Relative fit per episode

children.value: First step for three questions about questionnaire scores, asked per participant: do participants with higher scores (A) find the latent states earlier, (B) rely on them more once found, or (C) find them more often at all?

per episode: for each episode, the held-out log-likelihood per trial of a model with latent states minus that of the delta-rule tracker (nats per trial; positive = the model with states predicts the allocations better). The two folds of the relative-fit analysis were refitted (odd episodes → evaluated on the even episodes and vice versa), so every episode’s value is held out (
; the summed values agree with the stored held-out fits, ρ = .98 to .99). Two comparisons: Nexus vs tracker and the n-state model (Zika et al., 2023) vs tracker.
: first episode from which the relative fit is positive in that episode and in at least 75 % of the remaining episodes (none = never);
: mean relative fit from the discovery episode on;
: change of the relative fit per episode.

A: discrete-time hazard of discovery (logistic, one row per participant and episode until discovery) ~ q_z + condition, and, among those who discover, the discovery episode ~ q_z + condition; B: reliance ~ q_z + condition; C: discovered (0/1) ~ q_z + condition (logistic). In None + Partial (condition: Partial vs None) and in all participants; uncorrected.

Results with p < .05 (of 50 tests per comparison: five questionnaires, five tests, two samples):

In None + Partial, neither the timing (A) nor the probability (C) of discovery was associated with any questionnaire in either comparison (all p ≥ .11). Where reliance (B) was associated, higher anxiety scores went with a smaller advantage of the model with states after discovery.

The relative fit of a single episode is noisy (a participant’s values vary by several nats per trial from one episode to the next), so the discovery episode is a coarse measure. For Nexus vs tracker, the discovery episode is earlier in participants who place nets on both directions more often after events (Spearman ρ = −.54 after transitions, −.57 after oddballs), and the mean relative fit is higher in them (ρ = .52 and .59), in line with the relative fit of Nexus being largely accounted for by hedging between learned directions (

). It is not related to the episode in which the colour-cue mapping is learned (ρ = .25, p = .13). Participants who reported noticing rules had a discovery episode more often (.79 of 52 against .47 of 34). For the n-state model vs tracker, the discovery episode is related to none of these measures (|ρ| ≤ .19). The Nexus-based discovery therefore mainly marks the onset of split placements, and neither version isolates the discovery of the latent states. Files:
